Stable air pressure. No weather-sensitivity effects expected.
Slight pressure change. Very sensitive individuals may notice mild fatigue.
Noticeable pressure drop. Commonly: headaches, increased irritability, reduced concentration – especially for weather-sensitive people, migraine sufferers, and those with old injuries.
Noticeable pressure rise. Some people react with sleep disturbances or inner tension.
Sharp pressure drop. Weather sensitivity likely pronounced: migraine, joint pain, scar/wound pain, and circulatory issues possible. Plan rest periods.
Sharp pressure rise. Some people report head pressure, ringing in the ears, or heightened tension.
Extreme pressure change. Physically demanding, especially for the chronically ill, elderly, or weather-sensitive. Reduce exertion today.
Dogs often notice pressure changes earlier than humans and may respond with heightened alertness or mild restlessness. If you\'re weather-sensitive yourself: shorter sessions, no precision work.
Increased sensitivity likely – in both dog and human. Your own stress level directly affects training quality. Favor routine exercises over new demands today. Prefer calm terrain walks.
Extreme weather change. Dogs may be noticeably more restless and harder to handle. Avoid forcing or intensive training demands today. Short, relaxed walks only.
The air feels dry and pleasant. No humidity-related effect.
Comfortable humidity. No notable effect on wellbeing.
Noticeable mugginess. Sweating cools less effectively. Increased thirst, slightly reduced performance during physical activity.
Pronounced mugginess. The body\'s thermoregulation is impaired. Greater strain on circulation. Stay well hydrated, move intense activities to cooler hours.
Extreme mugginess. Heat exhaustion possible. Strongly limit physical activity. Drink plenty, seek shade, monitor body temperature.
No mugginess-related restrictions on training or activity.
Dogs cool less effectively through panting in muggy conditions. Reduce speed training and intense fetching today. Plan water breaks.

In high humidity, dogs are significantly more prone to overheating than at the same temperature with dry air. Avoid intense exertion today, keep walks short, provide plenty of water and shade. Brachycephalic breeds (bulldog, pug, French bulldog) are especially at risk.

Extremely muggy conditions – acute overheating risk for dogs. Limit physical activity to a minimum (short bathroom walks). Signs of heat stroke: heavy panting, excessive drooling, coordination problems, lethargy → cool down immediately and see a vet.
Mild heat stress possible with sustained physical activity.
Moderate heat stress. Drink plenty, avoid midday heat. Those sensitive to circulatory issues should be especially cautious.
Significant heat stress. Avoid intense physical activity, stay in the shade, stay well hydrated. Heat cramps and exhaustion possible.
Extreme heat stress. Risk of heat stroke. Reduce activities to a minimum.
Watch water intake. Plan short breaks.
Move training to early morning or evening hours. Avoid asphalt – can burn paws. Plenty of water.
No intense training sessions. Shortest walks, maximum shade. Monitor body temperature and panting.
Take the dog out only for bathroom breaks. Acute risk of heat stroke. Brachycephalic breeds, older, and sick dogs are especially at risk.
Cool conditions, no critical cold stress.
Noticeable cold stress. Warm clothing needed, especially protecting hands, head, and feet.
Strong cold exposure. Frostbite risk with wind exposure and no protective clothing. Limit time outdoors.
Extreme cold danger. Frostbite possible within minutes on uncovered skin.
No critical cold stress for healthy dogs with an undercoat.
Short-haired, small, and older dogs: a coat is recommended. Check paws for salt and ice.
All dogs: keep walks short. Short-haired breeds: a coat is necessary. Clean paws after the walk and check for cracks.
Life-threatening cold, even for dogs. Take out only for bathroom breaks, as briefly as possible.
No special thermal stress. Pleasant conditions for outdoor activities.
Very good conditions for training and off-leash walks.
Low storm potential. No effect on wellbeing.
Elevated storm potential. Atmospheric instability can increase restlessness and discomfort, especially in weather-sensitive people.
High storm potential. Weather-related mood swings and circulatory discomfort possible. Plan to head back early.
Many dogs respond to atmospheric instability before storms with increased restlessness or anxiety – even without visible weather signs. Keep the leash on as a safety measure.
Storm anxiety: dogs can sense pressure changes and electrostatic buildup before storms. Limit walk duration, have a safe retreat ready. Do not let anxious dogs off leash.

HundeWildnis uses notifications for the following purposes:

• BLOG UPDATES:
So you're always informed when new blog articles are published.

• NAVIGATION & PACE TRAINER / VOLUME TRAINER:
So navigation, the pace trainer, and the volume trainer keep working reliably even when the display is off or the app is moved to the background (e.g. when your phone is in your pocket during training, or your hands need to be free). In this case, a persistent notification is shown to keep the location service active.
If notifications are disabled, NAVIGATION, PACE TRAINER, and VOLUME TRAINER only work while the app is in the foreground and the screen is active.

PRIVACY:
No personal data is transmitted to external servers for these notifications. You can enable, adjust, or disable this feature at any time in settings:
Your device - Settings - Apps - HundeWildnis - Notifications

For the HundeWildnis app to correctly run all features such as location services, photos, microphone, and notifications, certain permissions are needed. Here is an overview:

Used for determining your location, POI search, routing, navigation, local weather, the pace trainer, and optional geotagging of your daily notes.\n• Choose \'While using the app\'. Thanks to a foreground service, this feature stays active even with a locked screen, provided notifications are enabled for the app, which is a technical requirement for this.
Needed to take photos for your daily notes, add images from the gallery to your daily notes, or add a photo of your dog to the dog profile.

Needed for frequency analysis in the voice trainer. Your voice is analyzed only locally on your device, and the frequencies are shown graphically and in tables to track your progress. Audio data is never stored.

Notifications are needed to inform you about new blog articles. You can also enable notifications for the pace trainer to be warned when exceeding your target pace. You can also use notifications in the voice trainer to get feedback during communication training with your dog on successful communication. 
So navigation and speed monitoring keep working reliably even when the display is off or the app is moved to the background (e.g. when your phone is in your pocket during training, or your hands need to be free), a persistent notification is shown in this case to keep the location service active.
If notifications are disabled, NAVIGATION and PACE TRAINER only work while the app is in the foreground and the screen is active.

PRIVACY:
No personal data is transmitted to external servers for these notifications. You can enable, adjust, or disable this feature at any time in settings:
Your device - Settings - Apps - HundeWildnis - Notifications
Can be used for haptic feedback on warnings in the pace trainer and/or voice trainer.
⚙️ How to control notifications and permissions manually:

1. Open Android Settings.
2. Go to 'Apps' -> 'See all apps'.
3. Find 'HundeWildnis' in the list.
4. Tap 'Permissions' to manage camera, location, microphone, etc.
5. Tap 'Notifications' to manage all notification options.

The start page shows the functions as tiles in six groups: Mental Preparation, Training Tools, Outdoor Tools, Dog, Safety & Emergency, Information & Learning, App Service.
• At the bottom you switch between Start, Courses and Emergency.
• The menu at the top right gives access to language, settings, backup, instructions, permissions, privacy policy, imprint and About the app.
• The app is free, needs no account and contains no advertising.

All data you enter or the app generates (dog profiles, training sessions, notes, photos, measurements) is stored locally on your device. It only leaves the device when you actively share or export it, create a backup, or use the optional WebDAV synchronisation with your own server. You are responsible for sharing data with third parties.

The courses are stored in the app and can be read without an internet connection.

Details are in the privacy policy (menu at the top right).

Some functions need online services for which you set up your own access (menu → Settings):
• Weather: Under “Services & Servers …” you choose OpenWeatherMap (your own key) or Open-Meteo (your own server address, key if applicable). Without access the app shows no weather data.
• Route calculation: Enter your own free OpenRouteService key (openrouteservice.org).
• Nearby places (Overpass): No key required. The server address can be changed.
Keys are stored encrypted. Only https addresses are allowed.

Guided breathing exercise for you and your dog: four phases (inhale, hold, exhale, hold) of 4 seconds each.
• A growing and shrinking circle shows the current phase.
• Optional: vibration at each phase change and background music.
• The elapsed time is displayed.

Train your ideal walking speed.
• Choose a limit (2.5 / 3.0 / 4.0 km/h) and the measuring interval (30 or 60 seconds). You can change the limit at any time during a measurement.
• When the limit is exceeded, the app warns you by vibration and/or sound (switchable separately) and optionally by notification. To use this, enable notifications in the Android settings (Apps → HundeWildnis → Notifications).
• The measurement runs as a background service and records the route via GPS.
• Each measurement is saved in the history and can be exported as GPX, PDF or via Share. The GPX file can be opened in a navigation app.

Supports and trains your voice when communicating with your dog.
• Choose “Holistic training” with five target frequencies (108, 216, 324, 432, 648 Hz) or “Focus training” with one target frequency.
• The app gives immediate feedback by display, vibration and/or sound (switchable separately).
• After each session an evaluation is created. It is saved in the history and can be shared as a PDF.

Uses the microphone to measure the volume of your speech and assigns it to levels.
• After the session the evaluation shows duration, average, minimum and maximum level and the distribution across the levels.
• Sessions are saved in the history and can be shared as a PDF.
• The audio data is evaluated on the device only.

Configurable timer for training intervals.
• Active/rest time (10–120 s), 1–20 rounds and cool-down phase (0–300 s).
• Six quick profiles: Standard, Puppy, Senior, Energetic, Working dog, Rescue dog.
• Sound and vibration per phase.
• Progress is kept in the history. A completed session can be transferred to the training diary.

Document your training per dog in 18 training categories. The dog must first be created in the dog profile; several dogs can be created.
• Choose dog and category and see your training progress so far.
• “+ New training session” records duration, repetitions, success, distraction level, difficulty, location (GPS), weather (only with weather access set up), terrain and your own notes.
• Progress, trend, statistics and milestones are determined automatically.
• All sessions are listed in the history. Export as PDF or CSV; sessions can be deleted per dog.

Monthly calendar with your training days.
• Tap a day to see its entries.
• Plan activities in advance and get reminded by notification.
• The 7-day preview shows weather suitability as a traffic light (with weather access set up).

Advisory system that assesses whether the planned exercise is appropriate for your dog today.
• On first use a notice explains that your location (temporary only) and weather data are needed.
• The assistant guides you in five steps through weather, terrain, ground, training level and recommendation. Weather values can be corrected manually.
• The recommendation gives length or area, difficulty, estimated trail age and a preparation checklist. A traffic light shows suitability for all three disciplines.
• The map tool draws a route or search area on the map and pre-fills terrain and ground from open map data.
• Sessions are documented. Statistics and trend per dog, export as PDF or CSV.

Recommendations for playful activities with your dog.\n• The assistant asks about location, terrain, equipment and play content and turns this into a suggestion.\n• Sessions are documented. Statistics per dog, export as PDF or CSV.

Document training, observations and anything important with text, photos and geodata.
• Enter a title and note text.
• Optional: insert GPS coordinates and weather data (weather only with weather access set up).
• Attach photos from the gallery or via camera.
• “Save note” stores the note in the history.
• Export as PDF or GPX, sharing and deleting are possible.

Weather report for your location or a selected place. A weather access must be set up (see “Services & Servers”).
• Training weather index with weather-dependent tips.
• Current data: temperature, feels-like temperature, wind, humidity, precipitation, pressure, visibility, UV index.
• Daylight, twilight and moon phase.
• Temperature curve and forecast for 24 hours and 7 days.
• Air quality and pollen, weather favourites.
With the free OpenWeatherMap plan, the UV index, sunshine duration, pollen and the storm forecast are not available.

Two functions:\n• Lightning-thunder calculator (offline): Measure the seconds between lightning and thunder. The app calculates the distance and rates it as a traffic light. With follow-up measurements it shows the trend, approach speed and estimated arrival time.\n• Storm risk forecast (requires a weather access that has been set up).

Map with dog-relevant places, search and routing based on OpenStreetMap.
• Map: your location as a marker, zoom buttons, location button to centre the map.
• Categories: Choose a category (e.g. dog run, vet, drinking water, hiking trail, emergency). The app searches within 3 km (storm shelter 5 km) and shows the results on the map and as a list by distance. Areas and paths are drawn as outlines or lines.
• Text search for places and addresses.
• Two-tap logic: the first tap on a result shows information (distance, address, phone, opening hours, leash rules, if entered in OpenStreetMap). The second tap starts navigation.
• Routing: on foot, by bicycle or by car with distance and walking time. If you deviate by more than 30 m the route is recalculated. If no route is possible a dashed straight line is shown. Routing requires your OpenRouteService key.
• Save and sort favourites.
• Share location: sends your position as a link via the Android Share function.
Digital orientation aid for hikes and terrain.\n• Also shows the direction of the sun, moon and Polaris (updated every 30 seconds, calculated without an internet connection).
Shows the altitude above sea level via GPS and barometer.\n• Calibration via the GPS starting value.\n• For higher accuracy the QNH value can be retrieved.

Manage any number of dog profiles. The profile is required for the training diary, scent work, play & fun, pulse check and emergency assistant.

Data
• Basics: name, breed, sex, neutering status, date of birth (also month/year or year only), origin, colour, photo.
• Identification: chip number, tax number, Tasso number, pet passport (country, number).
• Health: vaccination status, further vaccinations, last deworming, last flea/tick protection, weight, shoulder height, body length, medical notes.
• Contacts: vet, liability and health/surgery insurance, owner, emergency contact.
• Care and behaviour: food, behaviour, personality traits with quick profiles.

Further functions
• Timeline: shared time with your dog with the activities recorded in the app.
• Heat cycle tracker.

Display, export, emergency
• View and edit the profile.
• QR code, PDF and Share: you select the entries. The recipient can scan the QR code, the PDF also contains a QR code, “Share” creates a text list for a target app of your choice.
• 🚨 EMERGENCY: creates an emergency report for the vet, animal clinic or animal rescue. Name, breed, sex and weight are pre-filled. Add symptom, description, GPS location and photos. “Send contact report” creates a PDF you can share immediately; an accompanying text contains the key details and the GPS location as an OpenStreetMap link.
• All data stays on the device and only leaves it when you export or share.

Guided measurement of pulse and breathing rate.
• 15-second measurements with automatic extrapolation per minute.
• Assessment based on shoulder height, plus recording of capillary refill time, mucous membrane colour, consciousness and exertion scenario.
• Transfer into the emergency report, history, CSV export.
• The values do not replace a veterinary examination.

Digital magnifier using the camera.
• Three filters: thermal view, inversion, high contrast.
• Tapping focuses, “freeze” holds the image.
• Images can be saved to the gallery.

Offline database of 56 poisonous plants.
• Seasonal warning, text search, filters by toxicity and season.
• Your own photos per plant.
• Linked to the emergency assistant.
• If poisoning is suspected: open the emergency assistant and contact a vet immediately.

Share your location in real time with trusted people, e.g. when hiking together. The transmission runs via a WebDAV server that you set up yourself. Without WebDAV credentials the function is locked and links to the WebDAV settings.
• After activation a background service runs. It transmits your location when you move and otherwise at longer intervals, and shows the locations of the other devices on a map.
• For each device the battery level and a freely selectable label are shown. Locations not updated for more than 10 minutes appear grey.
• With one tap a route to the shared location can be calculated.
• Exclude the app from battery optimisation so that sharing continues with the screen locked.

Quick help when every second counts. The emergency assistant can be opened via the tile and via “Emergency” in the bottom bar.
• Select the dog (with several dogs, via a selection).
• Choose “Accident” or “Illness” and determine the type of emergency (17 emergency types in total).
• Short yes/no questions assess the urgency.
• The first-aid guide shows symptoms, immediate measures, what to do / what not to do and notes on transport. Depending on the emergency, a CPR timer or a countdown timer appears.
• From the guide you create an emergency report as a PDF with location, dog profile and photos and share it directly with the vet, animal clinic or animal rescue.
The guide does not replace veterinary care. In an emergency, call a vet practice or animal clinic immediately.

41 courses with lessons on training, behaviour and everyday life with the dog, in German and English.
• The courses are stored in the app and can be read without an internet connection.
• Choose a course, then a lesson. Use “Previous lesson” and “Next lesson” to move on.
• The language follows the app language (menu → Language).

Read articles from websites you subscribe to yourself, for example blogs about dogs and the outdoors.

On a straight stretch of about 15 to 30 steps, a treat is placed at first with every step, later every second step. The dog waits at the start and follows the trail together with you on a calm "search" cue to the end. Don\'t feed beforehand so motivation stays high.

A longer trail with direction changes is laid and left to age for a few minutes before running it. An item to indicate is placed at the end. Difficulty can be increased through length, angles and trail age.
Using a worn item of clothing, the dog picks up a person\'s individual scent trail and follows it until they are found. Start with short distances and a fresh trail.
Food or treats are hidden in small containers in the grass or undergrowth. The dog searches, finds them and receives them with our help. The difficulty of the hiding spots can be increased gradually.
Treats in small containers are hidden in knotholes, bark crevices or woodpiles. The dog must search for and indicate them specifically. It receives the reward with our help.

A pinecone held in your hand for several seconds is thrown out among several similar ones. The dog must find that exact cone by its individual scent – an exercise in scent discrimination. Other suitable natural materials work just as well as pinecones.

On a loose, long leash the dog is allowed to sniff at length and at its own pace, with no goal or pace set. Beforehand, you hide a container of treats. Helps mental relaxation after more demanding exercises.
A familiar person hides behind trees or bushes. The dog is sent off and should find the person by scent, then is praised generously and played with.
Instead of the usual loop, a deliberately unfamiliar stretch is chosen and walked slowly and mindfully. New stimuli and scents increase mental engagement without any extra exercises being needed.

A ball, dummy or other sturdy toy is thrown, the dog may fetch it, and we play with the dog. Later on: a sit or down before the throw also serves as impulse control. Note: this doesn\'t have to be pure retrieving, and doesn\'t need to be.

A toy is thrown in open terrain, then you walk on a bit further with the dog before sending it toward the throw spot with an encouraging cue. Over time the dog remembers the location and route better and finds the item by scent increasingly faster.
A throw toy is thrown low and flat; the dog catches it in a low jump or off the ground. Start with throws close to the ground.
Several toys are thrown out at different distances, and the dog is sent to one, then sent on to the next. The varying distances increase the difficulty through the search needed to find each toy.

A prey toy on a long pole with a line is moved back and forth along the ground (for large dogs, better to use just a long line without the pole), and the dog chases and catches it. We play with the dog right away.
Take turns tugging on a sturdy tug toy. A clear alternation between pulling and yielding structures the game and prevents excessive escalation.
The handler runs a short distance away, the dog chases and is allowed to "catch" them. Immediately followed by play with the dog.

The dog learns to push a large exercise ball (or, for small dogs, an ordinary soccer ball) deliberately in one direction or toward a target. Start with the dog deliberately touching the ball with its nose.
Unstructured play with a familiar, compatible playmate, without commands. Regular breaks let the dog self-regulate.

The dog trots at a steady pace next to the handler over a longer distance. Pace and distance are increased gradually to build basic fitness. The dog is kept motivated throughout, and the session finishes with a good round of play.
Weave in a zigzag between closely spaced trees or shrubs, varying the pace. Can be enriched into a heeling exercise with sit, down and stand.
A small slalom course is laid out on the ground using branches, stones or pinecones. The dog first works the slalom together with the handler, and once training progresses, also on its own.
Walk at a slow pace along a wide, fallen tree trunk or downed branch. The dog is guided calmly on the leash (later off-leash as training progresses).
Climb at a walk over an uneven tangle of roots or a rocky patch. Builds footing confidence and body awareness on uneven ground.
A controlled jump onto a low, stable tree stump or wall, holding a brief sit or stay there before stepping back down in a controlled way.
Crawl under a park bench or a low branch. Builds body awareness and agility in tight situations.
A simple course with a slalom, crawl-through tunnel and low elements is built from cushions, cones, hoops and poles for the dog to work through.
In a designated sandy area, toys or treats (in containers) are buried. The dog is allowed to dig specifically in that spot, without digging up the rest of the garden.
In a permitted spot with loose soil, treats (in containers) are buried shallowly for the dog to dig up freely.
A course with many hiding spots for treats or toys is built from boxes, buckets, blankets and tubes for the dog to search freely.
Several familiar toys are hidden around the area. The dog is guided or sent to each toy in a fixed order, one after another, until after days or weeks it keeps to the order on its own.
From increasing distance, switch between sit, down and stand using a visual or verbal cue, without the dog walking back to the handler.
The dog is placed freely at growing distance on a long line or in a secured area and is called back under increasing, harmless distraction.
Deliberately walk past controllable, harmless stimuli, rewarding the dog with a treat or toy for calm behavior afterward.
Settle Training in a Stimulating Environment
In an out-of-the-way spot in a park with foot traffic nearby, an extended settled position is taken up and held.
A floating toy is thrown into the shallow water of a stream or lake; the dog wades or swims in and brings it back. The water eases the load on the joints.
On hot days, play with a gentle stream of water from the garden hose; the dog may snap at the water or run through it.
Treats (in containers) are placed in hollows within a snow mound. The dog searches and brings them out one by one.
Bits of food are hidden between the fabric strips of a snuffle mat. The dog sniffs and roots them out one by one.
The dog\'s food or individual treats are hidden in different rooms. The dog searches independently. Difficulty rises with more hiding spots and a longer time delay.
A treat is placed in each cavity of a muffin tin, covered with tennis balls or other suitable objects that cannot be swallowed. The dog has to move the covers aside to reach the food.
A cardboard box or laundry basket is filled with crumpled paper, with treats distributed between the layers. The dog roots through it and searches.
Empty cardboard tubes are placed in a basket with treats distributed between them. The dog searches through the tubes one by one.
Treats are rolled into a blanket or towel or tucked into its folds. The dog has to unroll or root through the blanket to find them.
Treats are wrapped in plain packing paper, folded several times and optionally tucked into an empty cardboard tube. The dog opens the parcel by itself.
Food or treats are stuffed into a Kong or food ball. The dog has to roll, push or chew it to reach the contents.
A commercial puzzle toy with drawers or flaps that must be opened or moved to reveal treats. Start at a low difficulty level.
An empty plastic bottle is given a few holes and filled with treats. The dog has to roll it with its nose or paw to make food fall out.
The dog waits in a sit or stay while its favorite toy is hidden in another room. It then searches for and retrieves it on command.
A family member hides in another room, and the dog is sent off on a signal to find them.
A ball or soft toy is rolled across the floor or thrown a short distance; the dog brings it back on cue, or we go to it to play together. Sitting calmly before the throw is a fixed rule.
Tug-of-War With a Rope or Fleece Toy
Pulling together on a rope or fleece tug toy, with the handler or the dog winning in alternating turns.
A small course with a slalom, a tunnel and a low hurdle is built from chairs, blankets and a broom handle on buckets for the dog to run on command.
Broom handles are laid low between two supports. The dog walks deliberately over the poles at a walk without touching them – trains coordination and body awareness.
The handler stands with legs apart and guides the dog with a treat back and forth through the legs in alternating steps.
The dog learns to stand on a stable stool or cushion with its front or hind paws. Specifically builds body awareness.
The dog learns to climb stairs at a walk and on command in a controlled way instead of rushing – a brief sit before each step, then "on".
Two or three overturned cups are set out, with a treat hidden under one. The dog indicates the correct cup with a paw or nose. Positions are then shuffled.
The dog learns to press its nose against a hand target or a marked object. A foundation for many further trick sequences.
The dog sits and places its paw in the handler\'s hand on cue – a classic trick command and the basis for further tricks.
Trick Sequence: Spin, Roll Over, Back Up
Building on basic obedience, tricks such as spinning in place, lying down and walking backward are trained using treat luring.
A fixed name is introduced for two or three familiar toys. The dog learns to pick out the named object from several and bring it.
The dog learns to pick up individual toys and place them in a box or basket. Combines prey play with target-object training.
The dog learns to nudge doors shut or bring small items such as a newspaper or slippers. Builds on target and retrieve training.
Naturally occurring behavior such as lying down, spinning in a circle or a head movement is marked and rewarded the moment it happens, so it can later be put on cue.
The dog lies or sits while a treat is placed on its nose or paw. It has to wait for the release cue instead of eating it right away.
Impulse Control: Treat in the Fist
A treat is offered in a closed fist. The dog must not snap or paw at it; the hand only opens and rewards once the dog is calm.
Impulse Control: Treat by the Paw
The dog holds a sit or down while a treat is placed in front of its paws and may only be eaten after the release cue.
The dog is lured onto a fixed mat with treats; staying there is built up and later linked to a settle cue. Duration and distraction are increased gradually.
The dog lies calmly next to the handler and is stroked while being spoken to calmly at the same time. Over several weeks this builds an automatic relaxation response to the cue.
A sit, down or stand is commanded, and the dog must hold the position while the handler moves away or adds distractions, until the release cue.
Basic commands are performed over increasing distance between dog and handler, first using body language, later purely verbally.
Free Play Without a Training Goal
The handler invites the dog to play freely through body language, with no commands or performance goal, purely physical and in a relaxed atmosphere.

Why do I need my own access?
The app has no weather server of its own and does not ship weather data. Weather services only allow requests with a personal key (API key). With your own key, the limits and terms of your account with the provider apply, and requests go directly between your device and the provider. The app developer does not see them.

Recommended to start: OpenWeatherMap
1. Open openweathermap.org and create a free account (button below). Confirm your email address.
2. Sign in and open the "API keys" section of your account. A key ("Default") already exists. It has about 32 characters.
3. Copy the key, choose "OpenWeatherMap" here and paste it into the field. Tap "Done".
4. A new key is often active only after a few minutes, sometimes after one or two hours. If the app reports that the key was rejected, wait a while and try again.

Notes
• The free plan is enough for the app. Do not book a paid plan.
• Treat the key like a password and do not share it. The app stores it encrypted on your device.
• With OpenWeatherMap's free plan, UV index, sunshine duration, pollen and the thunderstorm forecast are not available. The app hides these displays.
• The weather view names the provider as the source ("Weather data © OpenWeather").

Open-Meteo
Open-Meteo is meant for users who have a customer access with their own server address and key (open-meteo.com) or run their own server. The free Open-Meteo address is only permitted for non-commercial use; whether your case qualifies is for you to check in Open-Meteo's terms. Enter the address (and, if you have them, the air quality address and key) exactly as the provider gives them to you. With Open-Meteo all weather displays are available.

Overpass (nearby places, surroundings) For searching nearby places and for surroundings data on the map, the app queries the Overpass API. You need no key and no account. By default the app uses public Overpass servers (overpass-api.de and overpass.private.coffee) that all users share. They are free but limited: under heavy load they respond slowly or reject requests. The app then switches to the other server automatically. If you search often or searches fail often, enter the https address of another public server or of your own server under "Overpass server". If something is entered there, the app uses only that server. The operator's usage policy applies. If you leave the field empty, everything stays as described.
